description: We are a small team interested in AI, coding, space and real world data. We have worked on AI projects, web apps, maps and hackathons. For NASA Space Apps, we want to build a useful solution for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Looking for teammates interested in GIS, remote sensing, planetary science, data, UI/UX or research. Good teamwork and active contribution is most important.
summary:
VICTOR is a web tool for looking at and planning out possible Marswalk routes around Jezero Crater. The idea was to bring the terrain and the science targets together in one place rather than have someone go between a number of different maps.

The planner evaluates four different route options: one that puts a higher weighting on hazards, one that puts a higher weighting on distance, one that puts a higher weighting on science priority areas and one that is a more balanced approach. You can of course change your start and end points, switch map layers, compare route distance and estimated time and look at why a particular route segment has been scored as it has.

The Jezero map is based on MOLA elevation, THEMIS night infrared, MRO CTX and CRISM spectral indices. Published science targets and archived Perseverance/MEDA data provide the context. Some of the layers have gaps and some of the scores are modelled so VICTOR is a prototype for exploration planning only and is not a system that would be certified for use in actual astronaut operations.
details:
VICTOR is a web app to look for possible Marswalk routes around Jezero Crater. We selected Jezero for the lake and delta deposits because it is a fascinating setting for research and safe mobility.

Study Area: 18.0-18.9°N, 77.0-78.0°E We make the regional data onto 300 × 300 grid so that the layers can be compared with the same map.

The four datasets have separate functions. MOLA gives us elevation for calculating slope and traversability. THEMIS night-infrared brightness is normalized (we use it as a relative index of thermal inertia, not as a temperature measurement.) CTX is the visual background imagery. CRISM OLINDEX3 and CINDEX2 spectral indices fill in part of the science layer. Since not all places on the planet are covered by CRISM, we leave places without measurements as no-data instead of places lacking minerals.

Published Jezero science-target locations are also used as a science-priority layer. These scores are model outputs, not the actual magnitude of mineral abundance. We've maintained that distinction in our application.

A algorithm which generates 4 alternative routes: SAFEST, FASTEST, SCIENCE-RICHEST and BALANCED. The routes are represented in comparison using distance, estimated travel time, hazard and science scores. The user has the ability to select a route segment and view its input maps and the contributing factors to the cost for that segment.

Furthermore, a K-means terrain classification layer was added to help visualize the general terrain trends. This layer is to provide context only, so the route processing is not based on this data. In the environment, you can find the archived Perseverance MEDA information; this data is for historical context only.

The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Leaflet and Recharts. The backend uses FastAPI and Python, with geospatial and scientific libraries for data processing. We considered source resolution, incomplete coverage, Mars-specific coordinates and the need to distinguish measured data from modelled results.

VICTOR is designed to aid exploration and comparison. Its travel-time and hazard models are very simple and do not substitute for a full astronaut suit, or a mobility or life-support model.
